To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
environmental effects on galaxy properties have little impact on constraining cosmological parameters from galaxy clustering statistics.

environmental effects have a significant impact on real-space and, to a lesser degree, redshift-space clustering statistics, which can be explained in terms of the age and richness dependence of halo clustering, and that this effect is not large enough to significantly bias cosmological constraints from halo occupation distribution modeling.

the environmental effects on the clustering of SAM galaxies can be understood by decomposing the 3D correlation function into components based on the origin of galaxy pairs, and the effect on the clustering of the most affected SAM luminosity sample can be as large as 10% if environmental effects on galaxy formation are neglected in the modeling of the real- and redshift-space 2PCF.
In summary, our research is concerned with
environmental effects on galaxy correlation function.
the environmental impact on galaxy clustering, which is important for the interpretation of galaxy clustering statistics in cosmological studies.
the impact of environmental effects on the clustering of galaxies, and the effect on the measurement of clustering statistics from the Millenimum Simulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the environmental effects are not significant for constraining the cosmological parameters, and the effect is smaller than 10% for the 2PCFs of the luminosity-threshhold samples we examined.
the environmental effects are small, and the effect on the 2PCFs can be well understood and corrected for.
the environmental effects on galaxy properties are important for the most luminous galaxy sample, and less significant for the less luminous samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
environmental effects are important for galaxy clustering studies, and the effect can be quantitatively estimated with a simple method, as demonstrated in this work.
the environmental effects on real-space galaxy clustering statistics can be well understood by decomposing the clustering into different components.

environmental effects can be neglected in constraining cosmology from galaxy clustering, and that the method presented in the Appendix can be applied to decompose the two-point correlation function of a volume-limited sample into the two-point autocovariation and cross-correlation of galaxy subsamples, and to measure the two autocorrelation functions and the cross-correlation function simultaneously.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the environmental effects on galaxy 2PCFs can be quantitatively understood in terms of halo clustering.
environmental effects are not a major source of systematic uncertainty in construing cosmological constraints from the 2PCFs of luminous galaxy samples.

the environmental effects on the 2PCFs of luminosity-threshold galaxy samples can be well understood by the age and galaxy occupation number dependence of the 2PCFS of dark matter halos and the correlation between galaxy properties and halo age.
